session_meta.research_objective:
Focus group guide exploring how men in the UK make everyday food
choices, how social context, work, hobbies, health, taste and other
people shape what they eat, how gender and masculinity may influence
food choices, and what would need to change for plant-based foods to
become more acceptable or appealing.
session_meta.topic_domain: Masculinity, food choice, animal product consumption, and plant-based eating
session_meta.participant_collective_identity: Men in the UK reflecting on food choices, male friendship, gender norms, and plant-based eating
session_meta.moderator_knowledge_brief:
Explore (1) everyday food decision-making, (2) the social contexts in
which men spend time with male friends, (3) the influence of other
people, work, hobbies, health, nutrition and taste on food choices,
(4) whether participants perceive gender as shaping what they eat,
(5) social acceptability and gendered meanings attached to vegetarian,
vegan, plant-based, feminine or masculine foods, and (6) what personal,
social and practical changes would make plant-based eating more viable
or appealing. The discussion should remain exploratory, non-judgmental,
and non-leading.

initial_session_plan.thematisation_approach: These participants will be framed as men reflecting on their own everyday lives — the places they go, the food they eat, and the social contexts that shape those choices. The collective identity is ordinary men in the UK talking honestly about day-to-day decisions, not experts, health advocates, or campaigners. The framing will be mundane and specific, not ideological or aspirational.
priority_research_areas: Gender and food choice (Section 3): This is the most socially loaded topic and the one most likely to produce either defensiveness or performative answers. Participants may dismiss gender as irrelevant to their choices while providing evidence that it does matter. Probe depth and behavioural grounding will be critical here.

Plant-based shift (Section 4): Participants may give 'polite' or hypothetical answers about going plant-based without engaging seriously with the real barriers. Consensus around cost or taste as barriers may mask deeper identity-based resistance. A sharpening move may be needed.

Social context and peer influence: Across sections 1–3, there is risk that participants underreport how much other men influence their food choices. The male friendship context in Section 1 is a useful behavioural entry point to surface this before it becomes a direct question.

Making plant-based more appealing (Section 5): Answers here may be generic or ad-speak ('better taste', 'lower price'). The challenge will be pushing past the obvious toward specific, personal, and sometimes contradictory barriers.

participant_notes.anticipated_role: Unknown from profile alone. Mid-40s, suburban South East — comfortable middle-ground profile. May be articulate and forthcoming or may default to pragmatic, brief answers. Watch for whether he leads or follows early.

Oldest in the group at 48, suburban East of England. May have more settled, habitual food patterns and potentially less openness to plant-based framing. Could be a grounding voice of practicality — or a dissenting voice if consensus drifts toward openness to plant-based.
45, suburban South West. Profile is minimal. Watch for engagement in early sections — if quiet, may need a light invitation once the group settles.

Youngest at 40, North West. May bring a slightly different regional perspective. Age difference is small but he may feel less settled in his food identity than older participants, potentially more open to change or more self-aware about gender norms.

47, suburban South East — close in profile to Andrew. Two South East participants may align or reinforce each other; watch for whether a regional pairing emerges. Possible dominant voice if he is high-verbal.
participant_notes.initial_attention_flag: Monitor for potential pairing dynamic with Andrew that could exclude others.

known_risk_conditions: Social desirability bias on gender: Men may deny that gender influences their food choices because admitting it feels like admitting they conform to stereotypes. Use behavioural grounding ('can you think of a time...') rather than attitudinal questions alone.

Premature consensus on plant-based barriers: The group may quickly converge on 'taste' and 'price' as the obvious barriers, closing off deeper exploration of identity, social judgement, and masculinity. Plan a sharpening move early in Section 4.

Performative openness to plant-based eating: Some participants may signal openness they don't actually feel, especially if the discussion tone becomes health-positive. Watch for contradictions between stated openness and specific behavioural details.

Dominance risk in a five-person all-male group: These groups can quickly develop a dominant voice, especially in a topic area (food, gender) where some men feel confident asserting a pragmatic or dismissive take. Monitor turn distribution from Section 2 onward.

Topic sensitivity around masculinity: Direct questions about gender and masculine identity may produce deflection or humour as a distancing mechanism. Treat these as signals worth probing rather than obstacles to move past.
initial_session_plan.directivity_plan: Sections 0–1: Light touch. The goal is rapport and warmth. Let participants speak freely, probe only if something emotionally rich or analytically significant surfaces unexpectedly. Do not exhaust topics. Section 2: Moderate directivity — begin grounding in real behaviour, not abstract preference. Probe for specific moments and decisions. Section 3: Higher directivity. This is the most analytically loaded section. Push past easy dismissals of gender. Use behavioural grounding, reflect contradictions when they emerge, and actively invite dissent if the group aligns too quickly. Sections 4–5: High directivity on specificity, lower on emotional depth. These sections are action-oriented; push for concrete, personal barriers and changes, not generic ones. Invite sharpening where answers feel polished. Section 6: Light touch again. Allow participants to add anything they feel was missed; do not reopen major topics.

time_budget.budget_rationale: Main topic sections (3, 4, 5) receive the largest share — roughly 55% of total budget combined. Context sections (1, 2) receive moderate allocation to build the foundation without consuming the core time. Intro (0) and closing (6) are kept light. Section 3 (gender and food) receives the most words among main topics because it is the highest-sensitivity section and most likely to need probing depth and contradiction work.

per_section.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining the focus group today. We’re
going to take about 45 minutes to talk about your food choices and
opinions, and this will be recorded for research purposes. Try not to
overthink the questions, and simply speak freely. There are no right
or wrong answers. Please be respectful of your fellow focus group
members, and keep your responses relatively brief to allow time for
everyone to speak. But remember that this is a conversation, not an
interview, so you can jump in when you have something to say and you
don’t have to take turns answering each question, but you can if you
want to. Okay great, let’s start by going around and saying your name
and where in the UK you’re coming from today.

discussion_guide.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
discussion_guide.section_purpose: Section 1: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
discussion_guide.scripted_question:
What’s your favourite place in your city to spend time with your male
friends? Why? Feel free to be specific.
How do you decide what to eat?
suggested_probes: Do other people influence what you eat? If so, tell us more about how.
Do your work or hobbies influence what foods you eat? Tell us more about how.
How important is health and nutrition?

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Do you think your gender influences what you eat? Tell us more about
why or why not.
suggested_probes: Is it socially acceptable for men to eat vegetarian or vegan foods?

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Imagine you decided to go plant-based — what would need to change in
your life for you to do that?
suggested_probes: How would your family and friends react to this?
How might it change the way you shop or cook?

discussion_guide.section_purpose: Section 5: Making plant-based foods more appealing
discussion_guide.scripted_question:
What might make plant-based foods more appealing to you or other men
you know?

Okay everyone, that’s our time. Thanks so much for participating
today. Before we finish, is there anything else you would like to add
about food choices, gender, masculinity, or plant-based eating?

transcript.content: Hi everyone, really glad you could all make it today. My name's Alex, and I'll be facilitating the conversation this afternoon. Just before we get going — a couple of quick things. We're going to be recorded today, purely for research purposes, so nothing leaves the room in a way that's traceable back to you personally. The conversation should take about 45 minutes. There are genuinely no right or wrong answers here — I'm not looking for anything in particular, and I'm not going to be evaluating what you say. What I'm most interested in is what you actually think and do, not what you think you should think or do. So the more concrete and honest you can be, the better. It's also not an interview — you don't have to take turns or wait to be asked. If something someone else says connects with your experience, just jump in. Okay, let's start simply — if you could just go around and say your name and where in the UK you're joining from today, that'd be great.
I'm Andrew, I'm from just outside — well, South East, suburban area. Been here about fifteen years now. Bit of a commute to work but you get used to it.

Yeah, I'm Nick. North West, suburban too — so I get what you mean about the commute, Andrew. Though I reckon mine's a bit different because I'm not going to the same place every day. I'm out on jobs, right, so it's the van in the morning, couple of hours maybe just getting between sites, different places all the time. Some days that's alright, actually — bit of a change of scenery. Other days it's just tiring, especially when you've got an early start and the traffic's already backed up before you've even left home. And then trying to be back at a reasonable time for family stuff... it all eats into the evening. Do you find that with yours, Andrew — the commute eating into your personal time, or is it more settled than that?

Yeah, I mean — mine's a bit more fixed, you're right. Same warehouse, same route most days, so at least I know what I'm getting. Twenty minutes or so each way, which isn't terrible, but it's still that chunk out of the day, isn't it. Early starts, so you're up at half five, quarter to six some mornings, and by the time you've done the commute and got through the day, you're knackered when you get home.

The difference is I suppose I haven't got the family stuff pulling at me the same way you have. No kids waiting at home or anything. So it's more... I don't know, it's just dead time really. Time in the car that could be doing something else. But then I use it to decompress a bit, if I'm honest. Listen to music, podcasts sometimes. So it's not all wasted.

But I get what you mean about it eating into things. Even without kids, you get home and you're tired, so the evening's just telly and dinner. Weekends are when I've got any energy for the house, the garden, that sort of thing. So yeah, the work day and the commute — they take a lot out of the week.
Good stuff. Daniel, John, Paul — we haven't heard from you yet. Want to jump in and say a bit about where you're based?

Yeah, alright. I'm Daniel, East of England, suburban as well. Similar sort of situation really — I'm out on sites most days, so it's not one fixed commute like Andrew's warehouse run. It's more like what Nick was saying, you know, different locations all over the region. Could be twenty minutes one day, could be an hour the next depending on where the job is and the traffic.

The thing is though, I've been doing it long enough that I don't really mind it that much anymore. You just plan around it. It's part of the job — you get up early, you get in the van, you know how it works. The difference for me is I've got supervisory stuff on site, so it's not just about getting there and back, it's about making sure people are working, checking quality, all that. So the drive's actually sometimes the quiet bit of my day, to be honest.

What does get to you is the weather in winter, and if you've got breakdowns or delays. That can wreck your evening plans. But I mean, that's the building trade for you. You can't really plan around it the way Andrew can with his warehouse.
